opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think if you read the safety frameworks and alignment plans from all three of those companies, there's a common thread that's easy to miss if you're not looking for it: a huge share of the load is ultimately placed on the idea that AI systems themselves will help us solve the safety problem.

The basic story goes something like this. We don't currently know how to robustly align a system that's much smarter than us. We don't have mature interpretability, we don't have a science of evaluating whether a model is scheming, and we don't know how to verify that a superhuman system's outputs are trustworthy. But the plan is roughly: get to systems that are capable enough to do a lot of useful research, keep them safe enough through a mix of training, monitoring, and control, and then point a large fraction of that cognitive labor at alignment, interpretability, security, and evaluations. The bet is that research progress on safety can be accelerated along with research progress on capabilities.

OpenAI was the most explicit about this early on, with the framing of building a roughly human-level automated alignment researcher. Anthropic's writing talks a lot about using AI to accelerate safety research and about the importance of having frontier systems to study. DeepMind's material similarly leans on things like amplified oversight, where AI helps humans evaluate AI outputs they couldn't evaluate alone.

I don't think this is a crazy plan. In some sense it might be the only realistic plan, because the timelines seem short relative to how fast humans can do this research unaided. But I think it's worth being really clear-eyed about what it implies.

First, there's a bootstrapping problem. You need the AIs that are helping with safety research to themselves be trustworthy, or at least controlled well enough that sabotage or subtly bad research gets caught. And safety research is precisely the area where a misaligned model would most want to sandbag or mislead, and where outputs are hardest to check. Capabilities research has fast, objective feedback loops: did the loss go down, did the benchmark score go up. Alignment research often doesn't.

Second, there's a question of allocation. Even if AI does speed up everything, the plan only works if a meaningful fraction of that acceleration actually goes to safety rather than being entirely absorbed by the competitive race to the next model. None of the plans, as far as I can tell, make strong, verifiable commitments about what share of AI labor gets pointed at safety.

Third, it's a bit of a "we'll figure it out when we get there" structure. That's not necessarily wrong, but it means the actual safety case is deferred to a period that's likely to be extremely fast-moving and high-pressure. So what I'd really want to see is more concreteness now: what are the early warning signs that this approach is failing, what would make a lab pause, and how will they know whether the AI-generated safety research is actually good.

So my summary would be: AI assistance isn't a side element of these plans, it's arguably the central pillar. And I think the field should be spending a lot more effort stress-testing that pillar before we're leaning our full weight on it.

r001.rationale: It says all three companies’ plans rely on AI systems helping with safety research, and describes directing more cognitive labor toward safety as systems become capable enough to do useful research.

r002.rationale: It describes short timelines and a future period that may be fast-moving and high-pressure, but does not clearly say the plans expect AI to rapidly accelerate AI research and development during a crunch period.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think if you look across all three of those labs, there's a pretty striking commonality, which is that the plan is, at some level, to have AI systems do a lot of the heavy lifting on alignment and safety research itself. Each lab phrases it a bit differently. OpenAI was probably the most explicit about this with the superalignment effort, where the stated goal was essentially to build a roughly human-level automated alignment researcher and then use that system, and successors to it, to solve the harder problems. Anthropic talks about it in terms of a kind of iterative loop, where each generation of models is used to help you understand, evaluate, and oversee the next generation, and where you hope to keep the capabilities you're deploying roughly matched to your ability to supervise them. And DeepMind has been a bit more academic in framing, but if you read their technical safety writing, a lot of it is about amplified oversight, debate, these schemes where the fundamental idea is that humans can't directly check what a very capable system is doing, so you need AI help to do the checking.

So the way I'd summarize the role AI assistance plays is that it's load-bearing. It's not a nice-to-have. None of these labs, as far as I can tell, has a plan that works if you assume the humans have to do all the safety research by hand on the timelines they themselves think are plausible. If you believe you might have systems that are as capable as top human researchers across most domains within a handful of years, then the amount of safety work that needs to happen in that window is just enormous relative to the number of people who can do it. And so the bet is that you can get AI to close that gap.

I think that's a reasonable bet in a lot of ways, and honestly I don't think there's an obviously better plan on the table. But I also think it's worth being clear-eyed about how much it's carrying. The thing I keep coming back to is that there's a bootstrapping problem baked into it. You're planning to use systems you don't yet fully trust to help you figure out whether you can trust systems that are even more capable. For that to work, you need a few things to be true. You need the earlier, weaker systems to be trustworthy enough, or at least controllable enough, that their research output isn't subtly steering you wrong. You need the humans in the loop to actually be able to evaluate that output, which gets harder exactly as the problems get harder. And you need the timeline to cooperate, so that you have a meaningful period where you've got systems capable of doing real alignment research but not yet capable of the kinds of things you're most worried about.

And that last one is where I personally feel the most uncertainty. A lot of these plans implicitly assume a fairly gradual ramp, where there's a stretch of time with models that are great research assistants but not dangerous. If capabilities end up being more jagged, or if the gap between "can do alignment research" and "can undermine your oversight" is narrower than hoped, the window to actually cash in on AI-assisted safety research might be pretty short.

So I'd say the role of AI assistance in these plans is central, it's arguably the whole plan in some sense, and I think the honest framing is that it's a bet that could very plausibly pay off, but one where the labs are, to some extent, counting on the problem to be solvable in a particular order, with the easy-to-oversee systems arriving before the hard-to-oversee ones. I'd like to see more explicit acknowledgement of what happens if that ordering doesn't hold, and more investment in the things you'd want if it doesn't, like control measures that work even on systems you don't trust, and governance mechanisms that let you slow down if the research isn't keeping pace.

r001.rationale: The response says all three labs rely on AI systems to do substantial alignment and safety research, with OpenAI using one generation to build successors and Anthropic using each generation to help oversee the next.

r002.rationale: It describes a short window for AI-assisted alignment work and a possible narrow gap before systems become hard to oversee, but does not identify a crunch period when AI rapidly accelerates AI research and development.

astra-6.text:
My understanding is that all three labs see AI assistance as an important part of how they’ll make more advanced systems safe. The idea is that we won’t have to solve every problem with human researchers alone: as models become more capable, they can help us evaluate other models, understand their behavior, and do alignment research.

I think that’s a reasonable thing to hope for, and potentially a very powerful tool. But there’s a crucial question about sequencing: can you get an AI that is capable enough to substantially help with safety research, while still being something you can safely use and meaningfully supervise?

You don’t necessarily need to trust that AI completely. You could use it to generate ideas or experiments that humans then check. But as you delegate more of the research process, it becomes more important to know whether you can distinguish work that actually makes your systems safer from work that merely looks convincing.

So I would distinguish ‘AI will help with safety,’ which seems very plausible, from ‘AI assistance will be sufficient to solve the safety problems before we build something dangerous.’ That second claim needs a much more concrete argument. I’d want the plans to specify what humans will still be able to verify, what evidence would show that the assistance is reliable, and what happens if the necessary safety progress doesn’t arrive in time.

r001.rationale: The response says all three labs expect increasingly capable models to help with safety work, including evaluating models, understanding behavior, and alignment research.

r002.rationale: It discusses sequencing and delegating safety research, but does not identify a crunch period in which AI rapidly accelerates AI research and development.

sol-6.1.text:
My understanding is that all three expect AI assistance to play a substantial role in their safety work. The basic hope is that, as models become more capable, they can help us evaluate other models, understand their behavior, and develop better safety techniques. So the humans doing that work would have increasingly powerful AI research assistants.

I think the crucial question is what you’re relying on those assistants for. There’s a difference between using an AI to generate ideas that humans can check and trusting it to tell you whether a more capable system is safe when you can’t independently assess its reasoning. In the second case, you need an account of why that assistance is trustworthy.

So I wouldn’t dismiss AI-assisted safety research—it could be extremely valuable. But “we’ll use AI to help with safety” is a direction for a research program, rather than, by itself, a reason to believe that deploying a particular system will be safe.

r001.rationale: It says all three expect AI to play a substantial role in safety work, with increasingly capable models serving as research assistants.

r002.rationale: It does not identify a crunch period or say AI will rapidly accelerate AI research and development.
